title: The project management plan & its stakeholders
blurb: What the project management plan covers, who writes and approves it, and every stakeholder who has a stake in it.
question: A project manager has drafted the project management plan for a leisure centre refurbishment. Before it is approved, who should be involved in shaping it, who approves it, and why does each of them care what it says?

teach.body: The project management plan (PMP) documents how the project will be delivered. It brings together why, what, how, who, when and how much: objectives, scope, schedule, budget, resources, risk, quality, communication, roles, governance and change control. The project manager writes, owns and maintains it; the sponsor approves it. Once approved, it acts as the agreement between the sponsor and the PM.

head: Question
What the PMP covers
rows: Objectives, linked to the business case
teach.caption: Communication arrangements also sit in the plan: who needs what information, when and how.

head: Stakeholder
Their stake in the PMP
rows: Approves it; it is the agreement with the PM
Release the people it relies on

teach.body: Sam, the PM, drafts the plan for refurbishing the pool and gym. The contractor supplies build durations; the PMO provides the template and checks it meets standards. The duty manager's line manager confirms which lifeguards can be released for training. The centre manager and swim club review the closure dates. Sam presents it to Alex, the sponsor, who approves it. From then on, it is the yardstick for delivery.

steps.label: Draft
steps.sub: PM writes it with input from team, suppliers, users

steps.label: Review
steps.sub: Stakeholders check it is realistic and complete

steps.label: Approve
steps.sub: Sponsor agrees and signs it off

steps.label: Deliver
steps.sub: Work is managed and reported against it

steps.label: Maintain
steps.sub: PM updates it when change control approves a change

teach.h: Involve stakeholders, or the plan won't hold
teach.body: A plan written alone is a guess. Team members and suppliers make estimates realistic; line managers commit the people; users make sure scope and handover meet their needs; the PMO keeps it to standard. Leave a stakeholder out and the plan may promise resources nobody agreed to, miss real requirements or clash with a contractor's capacity.

teach.h: Business case vs project management plan

teach.text: Common confusions: the SPONSOR approves the PMP but does not write or own it; the PMO supports and assures it but does not approve it; the team contributes but does not own it. And a group with no involvement in the project (an unrelated team, a competitor) is not a stakeholder of the PMP.

items: The PMP documents how the project will be delivered: why, what, how, who, when, how much.
The PM writes, owns and maintains it; the sponsor approves it. It is their agreement.
Stakeholders: sponsor, PM, team, governance board, users/customers, suppliers, PMO, line managers.
Involving them makes the plan realistic, committed and accepted.

summary: You can now explain what the project management plan covers and outline its stakeholders: the sponsor who approves it, the project manager who owns it, and the team, governance board, users, suppliers, PMO and line managers who shape and use it. You can also explain why involving each one makes the plan workable.

A.q: Which question does the project management plan mainly answer?
options: How the project will be delivered
Whether the investment is justified
Which benefits have been realised
Why the organisation needs change
A.why: The PMP documents how the project will be delivered: scope, schedule, budget, resources, controls and roles.

whyNot.1: Justifying the investment is the business case's purpose.
whyNot.2: Realised benefits are assessed in a benefits review.
whyNot.3: The need for change is set out in the business case.

A.q: Which pairing correctly describes ownership and approval of the project management plan?
options: Sponsor owns it; PM approves it
PMO owns it; board approves it
PM owns it; sponsor approves it
Team owns it; PM approves it
A.why: The project manager writes, owns and maintains the PMP; the sponsor approves it.

whyNot.1: The PMO supports with standards and assurance; it does not own the plan.
whyNot.3: The team contributes to and works to the plan, but does not own it.

A.q: Why are functional or line managers stakeholders of the project management plan?
options: They approve the plan for the sponsor
They provide the people it depends on
They own the schedule and the budget
They write the plan's quality section
A.why: Line managers release the people the plan relies on, so their commitment makes the resource plan realistic.

whyNot.2: The PM owns the schedule and budget within the plan.
whyNot.3: The PM writes the plan, with input from specialists.

B.q: Which of the following would NOT normally be a stakeholder of a project management plan?
options: The project management office
Suppliers delivering the work
Line managers providing staff
A team on an unrelated project
B.why: A team with no involvement in the project has no stake in how it will be delivered.

whyNot.0: The PMO provides standards and assurance for the plan.
whyNot.1: Suppliers deliver parts of the scope and must fit the plan.
whyNot.2: Line managers provide the resources the plan relies on.

B.q: What is the PMO's main interest in a project management plan?
options: Approving it on behalf of the sponsor
Owning and updating it during delivery
Checking it follows agreed standards
Writing the plan's detailed schedule
B.why: A PMO supports projects with standards, templates and assurance, so it checks the plan meets them.

whyNot.0: The sponsor approves the plan; a PMO supports, it doesn't approve.
whyNot.1: The PM owns and maintains the plan.
whyNot.3: Scheduling may get PMO support, but the plan is the PM's.

B.q: How do project team members relate to the project management plan?
options: They contribute to it and work to it
They approve it before the gate review
They own it once deployment begins
They have no part in it at any point
B.why: Team members provide estimates and specialist input, then carry out the work as the plan describes.

whyNot.2: Ownership stays with the project manager throughout.
whyNot.3: The team is a key stakeholder: their input makes the plan realistic.

C.q: A PM publishes the plan without consulting the contractor who will build the main deliverable. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The sponsor can no longer approve it
The plan may not match what can be built
The business case becomes invalid
The PMO must take over the plan
C.why: Without the contractor's input, durations, sequence and interfaces may be unrealistic.

whyNot.0: The sponsor can still approve it, but it may be a poor plan.
whyNot.2: The business case is not automatically invalid; the plan's realism is the problem.
whyNot.3: The PM still owns the plan; it needs the missing input, not a new owner.

C.q: Which THREE of the following would usually be stakeholders of a project management plan? 1. The sponsor 2. Team members 3. End users 4. A competitor's project manager
options: 1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
C.why: The sponsor, team members and end users all have a stake in how the project will be delivered.

whyNot.0: A competitor's PM has no role in your plan.
whyNot.1: A competitor's PM has no role, and team members are missing.
whyNot.2: A competitor's PM has no role, and the sponsor is missing.

C.q: Why is the approved project management plan described as an agreement between the sponsor and the project manager?
options: It transfers the sponsor's accountability to the PM
It records how the PM will deliver what was approved
It replaces the business case once deployment starts
It lets the PM change the approved baseline at will
C.why: The sponsor approves the plan, and the PM commits to delivering the project as it describes; changes then go through change control.

whyNot.0: The sponsor stays accountable; the plan doesn't move accountability.
whyNot.2: The business case remains the justification throughout.
whyNot.3: Changes to the approved baseline go through change control.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: You're having a new kitchen fitted. Who needs to see and agree the fitter's plan before any cupboards come out?

blocks.h: Everyone with a stake in the plan
blocks.body: The fitter (PM) writes the plan: what goes where, the order of work, the dates and the cost. You (sponsor) approve it. The electrician and plumber (suppliers) check their slots are realistic. Your family (users) check the layout works and when the kitchen will be out of action. Your employer (line manager) agrees days off to let trades in. Leave any of them out and the plan falls apart.

head: Person
Project role
Why they care
rows: Days off to let trades in

blocks.text: The fitter owns the plan; you approve it. If the fitter changes the order of works, they should check with you first: that's change control.

explain.body: The project management plan documents how the project will be delivered: objectives, scope, schedule, budget, resources, risk, quality, communication, roles, governance and change control.

test.q: Which of the following would you expect to find in a project management plan?
options: The post-project review findings
The approach to change control
The final benefits review results
The investment appraisal figures
test.why: How changes will be controlled is part of how the project will be delivered, so it belongs in the PMP.

whyNot.0: Post-project review findings come at closure, after the plan has done its job.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews happen after delivery and are reported separately.
whyNot.3: Investment appraisal is part of the business case.

explain.body: The PM creates the PMP with input from others, owns it and maintains it. When change control approves a change, the PM updates the plan so it stays current.

test.q: A change request is approved during deployment. Who updates the project management plan?
options: The project manager
The project sponsor
The PMO
The end users
test.why: The PM owns and maintains the plan, so they update it after an approved change.

whyNot.1: The sponsor may approve the change but does not maintain the plan.
whyNot.2: The PMO supports with standards and assurance; it doesn't own the plan.
whyNot.3: End users may be affected but don't maintain the plan.

explain.body: The sponsor approves the PMP, making it the agreement with the PM. The governance board, usually chaired by the sponsor, gives direction and reviews progress against the plan at decision gates.

test.q: What is the governance board's main interest in the project management plan?
options: Writing and maintaining it for the PM
Doing the work packages it describes
Testing the outputs it lists for defects
Giving direction and reviewing at gates
test.why: The board gives direction and makes key decisions at gates, using the plan to judge progress and readiness.

whyNot.0: The PM writes and maintains the plan.
whyNot.1: Team members carry out the work packages.
whyNot.2: Testing outputs is quality control, done by the team or inspectors.

explain.body: Team members, suppliers and contractors deliver work to the plan. Users and customers check requirements and handover. The PMO provides standards and assurance. Line managers release the people it relies on.

test.q: End users are stakeholders of the project management plan mainly because:
options: they approve the plan for the sponsor
they own the plan once handover starts
its scope and handover affect them
they write the plan's risk section
test.why: The plan defines what will be delivered and when it is handed over, which directly affects the people who will use it.

whyNot.1: The PM owns the plan throughout.
whyNot.3: The PM manages risk with team input; users don't write the plan.
